line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 Bd2 O-O a3 Bxc3
teaches: Giving up the bishop pair is a price, not a mistake, when what you buy is a permanent say over one central square. The knight being traded is a defender of that square; once it is gone, the pawn advance the whole opening is built on becomes hard to arrange, and the doubled pawns left behind cannot help with it either.
explains: The bishop takes on c3, removing the knight that was contesting the centre and leaving the recapture to damage the queenside pawns. The advance that would claim the middle now has one fewer supporter.
